title: Don't give up meeting (Hebrews 10:19–25)
hook: draw near; hold fast; stir each other up to love
tomorrow: how do you pack for a trip when nobody tells you where?

segments.voice: The new covenant: laws put into the mind and written on the heart, so that knowing God is like knowing a person. On their hearts. But a heart can still drift off alone.
screen: `ON THEIR HEARTS.` → `A HEART CAN DRIFT OFF ALONE.`

segments.voice: A tablet propped on a hospital tray table, the church service streaming, the choir a half-second out of sync with the picture. If you can pray anywhere, why does Hebrews care who shows up? Because some had already stopped. The letter says so, almost in passing: "Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is." As the manner of some is. Empty seats, already. The writer doesn't name anyone or scold them. Instead comes a reason, and it has nothing to do with taking attendance.
screen: `A SERVICE ON A TRAY TABLE.` → `AS THE MANNER OF SOME IS.` → `NOT ABOUT ATTENDANCE.`

segments.voice: First the passage opens a door: "Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus, By a new and living way." Then three invitations, each starting let us. "Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith." "Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering." And the third turns sideways, toward each other: "And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works." Provoke is usually the word for starting a fight. Here it's aimed at love. So does showing up in person still matter? Christians hold two honest views. The first: yes, bodies in one room. You can't consider someone you never see. A gathered church shares bread, sings out loud, and notices who's missing, and people who hold this view point to the word itself: assembling. The second: the gathering is wherever believers meet in his name. Jesus says, "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." For the sick, the homebound and the far away, people who hold this view say a kitchen table or a hospital room is a real gathering. Here's what both sides keep: the reason for meeting is each other, "exhorting one another," which means encouraging.
screen: `DRAW NEAR. HOLD FAST.` · `PROVOKE, AIMED AT LOVE.` · `VIEW ONE: BODIES IN ONE ROOM.` · `VIEW TWO: WHERE TWO OR THREE GATHER.` · then, large: `STIR UP LOVE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who used to show up, at church, at practice, in a group chat, and has gone quiet. Write them a short message with no guilt in it, only glad you exist. Hold it through the sit, and send it when it feels right.
Don't give up meeting. Hebrews ten: draw near, hold fast, and keep gathering, so you can stir one another up to love.
The line to keep: stir up love, provoke aimed the other way for once. Go well.

fork.setup: your friend says she worships online now and doesn't miss the building at all. you lean the other way. what's the best case for HER view?

chat.says: dad set up the livestream in pop's room sunday. pop says it's 'not the same.' is it church or not?
options: Christians differ: two or three gathered is real, and Pop still misses the faces that stir him up.
It's not church. Hebrews says watching from a hospital room counts as forsaking the assembling.
It's exactly the same. Hebrews only cares what you believe, not who you're sitting with.
chat.meaning: Jesus promised to be where two or three gather; Hebrews wants believers to consider one another. Both views hold that the gathering is for each other.

brethren.meaning: the King James word for fellow believers

the holiest.meaning: the inner sanctuary, the place nearest God

profession.meaning: here, what you openly confess you believe
